view.stem: Which complete arrangement obtains two coherent light beams for a stable interference pattern? Keep relative optical paths stable and the path difference compatible with the incident beam's coherence.

options.text: Switch on two unlinked ordinary lamps of the same colour together and overlap their beams; matching colour and start time keep the phase difference stable.
Split one beam into two parts, send them along different paths, and recombine them; the parts have the same frequency and a stable phase difference that need not be zero.
Split and recombine one beam; the parts are coherent only if their phase difference is exactly zero, and a fixed nonzero phase difference is incoherent.
Split one beam and change the frequency of one part; equal amplitudes preserve a stable interference pattern even when the two frequencies differ.

intent.task: Explain how to obtain coherent light waves and identify the frequency and phase relationship preserved by the method.
intent.source_solution: Split one beam into two parts, send them along different paths, and bring them together again. With stable relative optical paths and a path difference compatible with the beam's coherence, the parts retain the same frequency and a stable phase difference, supporting stable interference. Coherence does not require zero phase difference; two independent ordinary sources of the same colour or frequency do not by themselves guarantee a stable phase difference.
intent.unit_reason: The method and coherence criterion form one coupled experimental judgment. Select one complete arrangement rather than separate frequency and phase blanks; both the arrangement and its reason must be valid.
limitations: Recognizing a complete arrangement does not demonstrate unaided written recall or designing and building that arrangement.

rationales.derivation: Treat matching colour as matching frequency, then treat a shared switch-on time as permanent phase synchronization. Independent ordinary sources still have a time-varying phase relationship, so the inferred stability does not follow.
rationales.misconception: Infer a stable phase difference from matching colour and switch-on time, omitting the absence of phase linkage.

rationales.derivation: The parts inherit the incident wave's frequency and phase relationship. The stem's optical-path and coherence conditions preserve that relationship; a fixed nonzero phase difference still satisfies coherence.
Replace the condition of a stable phase difference with zero phase difference, then exclude every nonzero value. Coherence requires stability, not necessarily in-phase vibrations.
rationales.misconception: Equate coherence with being in phase and classify every fixed nonzero phase difference as incoherent.

rationales.derivation: Promote equal amplitudes, a condition for complete cancellation, into the whole coherence criterion. Unequal frequencies make the phase difference evolve in time, which equal amplitudes cannot prevent.
rationales.misconception: Substitute equal amplitudes for equal frequency and stable phase, overlooking phase drift from a frequency difference.

view.stem: Two coherent beams overlap in a non-absorbing region and form a stable bright-and-dark distribution. Which explanation correctly describes interference without treating darkness as disappearing light energy?

options.text: The separate intensities add directly everywhere, so the overlap becomes brighter at every position; phase difference changes timing but not brightness.
Opposing vibrations convert the beams' energy into heat at dark positions, while bright positions retain unconsumed energy, producing the pattern.
The vibrations superpose, and their phase relationship strengthens light at some positions and weakens it at others; dark positions receive less energy as energy flow is redistributed.
Overlap makes the frequency differ from position to position because of phase difference; those different frequencies, rather than resultant vibration size, create the bright-and-dark pattern.

intent.task: Explain strengthening and weakening through wave superposition, distinguishing local darkness from the disappearance of energy.
intent.source_solution: Where light waves meet, their vibrations superpose. Their phase relationship strengthens the resultant vibration at some positions and weakens it at others; coherent light can produce a stable bright-and-dark distribution. Vibrations add, so intensity is not simply the sum of the separate intensities everywhere. In the ideal case, opposite vibrations with equal amplitudes can cancel completely, whereas unequal amplitudes leave a remainder. Dark regions receive less energy, but interference neither destroys energy nor necessarily converts it to heat; it redistributes energy flow.
intent.unit_reason: The definition and the energy meaning of local weakening form one physical explanation. Keep them as one complete single-response judgment rather than separate clicks for strengthening, weakening, or energy.
limitations: Recognizing a complete explanation does not demonstrate composing an unaided written definition.

rationales.derivation: Replace coherent vibration addition with $I=I_1+I_2$, deleting the phase-dependent cross term. This yields brightness everywhere and cannot explain stable weakening in the overlap.
rationales.misconception: Add intensities instead of vibrations, losing the effect of phase on interference intensity.

rationales.derivation: Infer local energy consumption from a smaller resultant amplitude and label that consumption as heat. The region is non-absorbing; interference redistributes energy flow without supplying this heat conversion.
rationales.misconception: Treat local destructive cancellation as absorption and conversion to heat.

rationales.derivation: Coherent vibrations add according to phase and can strengthen or weaken the result; a stable phase relationship makes the distribution stable. Without absorption, darkness means less energy flow reaching that position, not destroyed energy.

Convert a spatial phase difference into a change in vibrations per second, then use the supposed frequency differences to explain brightness. A phase difference between equal-frequency waves is not a frequency change; resultant amplitude produces the pattern.
rationales.misconception: Confuse phase difference with frequency difference and replace superposition with frequency alteration.

view.stem: Compare the colours of single-frequency visible light and consider its passage across a stationary boundary between transparent media. Which statements hold? Select every statement that holds.

options.text: Colour differences of single-frequency visible light are associated with frequency; a wavelength specified in vacuum can also represent that frequency.
Single-frequency beams have different colours whenever their amplitudes differ; changing amplitude changes their spectral colour even at the same frequency.
Across a stationary boundary, frequency stays fixed while speed and wavelength may change; that wavelength change alone does not mean the single-frequency light changes colour.
Two single-frequency beams with equal measured wavelengths in different media necessarily have the same colour; their propagation speeds need not be known.

intent.task: Relate the colour of single-frequency light to frequency and handle the limitation of comparing wavelengths across media.
intent.source_solution: For the single-frequency visible light considered here, colour differences are associated with frequency; vacuum wavelength can also label that frequency. Crossing a stationary interface preserves frequency while speed and in-medium wavelength may change, so wavelengths measured in different media cannot be interpreted directly as a change of colour. Amplitude mainly concerns brightness and relative phase concerns interference; neither replaces the frequency distinction. This does not claim that the perceived colour of mixed light is determined by one frequency.
intent.unit_reason: The colour-related quantity and the validity of cross-medium wavelength comparisons jointly define one concept. One multiple-response judgment tests that relationship, rather than mechanically replacing a noun blank.
limitations: Recognizing the frequency explanation does not demonstrate unaided written recall of the relationship and its medium qualification.

rationales.derivation: Frequency is the lesson's colour distinction. In vacuum, $f=c/\lambda_0$, so the fixed vacuum speed lets vacuum wavelength label frequency without conflating wavelengths in different media.

Move from amplitude affecting intensity to amplitude determining spectral colour, mixing brightness with the frequency label. At the same frequency, amplitude changes do not change the light's spectral colour.
rationales.misconception: Mistake intensity or brightness changes for a change in the spectral colour of single-frequency light.

rationales.derivation: The boundary preserves frequency. Since $\lambda=v/f$, a change in medium speed changes wavelength while retaining the same frequency component; wavelength change alone is not recolouring.

Infer $f_1=f_2$ directly from $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$. In fact, $f_1=v_1/\lambda_1$ and $f_2=v_2/\lambda_2$; different media may have different speeds, so equal wavelengths alone do not establish equal frequencies.
rationales.misconception: Extend a same-medium wavelength-frequency comparison to arbitrary different media, dropping speed.

view.stem: After a transparent ice block is struck, some fractures show coloured glints in white light. Model one fracture as a very thin air gap, with suitable illumination and overlapping reflections from its two sides. Which explanation fits this thin-layer model?

options.text: The two reflections interfere, strengthening or weakening different frequencies by different amounts and changing the reflected colour proportions; gap thickness and viewing direction also affect the glints.
Light changes speed on entering the air gap, so its original frequencies change too; these new frequencies create the coloured glints, without a role for the reflections' phase relationship.
The reflections simply add intensities at every frequency, so gap thickness cannot affect colour proportions; the glints depend only on the incident light's colour proportions.
Ice fractures directly follow the green coating's quarter-wavelength rule; every fracture cancels the green component of white light in the same way, leaving fixed coloured glints.

intent.task: Under explicit conditions, explain coloured ice-fracture glints by interference of reflections from the two sides of a thin air layer, without asking the learner to make fractures.
intent.source_solution: Model an already observed fracture as a very thin air gap, with suitable white-light illumination and reflections from its two sides able to overlap. The two reflected waves come from the same incident light but follow different paths; their relative phase depends on gap thickness, viewing angle, wavelength, and reflection phase changes. Different frequencies in white light are strengthened or weakened by different amounts, changing the colour proportions of the remaining reflection and allowing coloured glints. The fracture is not a light source and need not convert light into new frequencies. Not every fracture has the necessary gap and overlap conditions, so the effect is not guaranteed. The ice-air-ice interface sequence differs from air-coating-glass, so the green antireflection coating's quarter-wavelength rule cannot simply be reused; the source also supplies no data for a unique numerical gap thickness.
intent.unit_reason: The gap structure, superposed reflections, and reflected colour proportions form one causal chain. Keep one complete single-response explanation rather than isolated recognition of an air gap and the word interference.
limitations: Recognizing the complete mechanism does not demonstrate building the thin-layer model or writing its conditional explanation unaided; no gap thickness is measured and no fracture is made.

rationales.derivation: Two reflections of the same incident light take different paths. Path difference and reflection phase changes determine relative phase, which varies with wavelength, thickness, and angle; the reflected intensities of white-light frequency components therefore differ, producing conditional coloured glints.

Incorrectly keep wavelength fixed across the boundary, use $f=v/\lambda$ to turn the speed change into a frequency change, and attribute colour to new frequencies. A stationary boundary preserves frequency and changes wavelength; the thin-layer model instead needs phase-dependent interference.
rationales.misconception: Hold wavelength fixed when medium speed changes, falsely altering frequency and removing reflected interference.

rationales.derivation: Add the separate intensities at each frequency and remove the phase term, giving a result independent of path difference and gap thickness. This deletes the thin layer's frequency-selective strengthening and weakening.
rationales.misconception: Add coherent reflections as incoherent intensities, denying the colour effect of thickness and path difference.

rationales.derivation: Transfer the green-light rule for the stated air-film-glass index sequence to ice-air-ice, then assume every gap already has the required thickness. Reflection phase conditions and actual gaps differ, so neither a universal thickness nor identical glints in every fracture follows.
rationales.misconception: Drop the reflection-phase conditions and actual thickness, treating a particular coating rule as universal for all thin layers.

view.stem: Natural light enters water from air and its wavelength becomes $\lambda_{\mathrm{water}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{air}}/n$, where $n$ is water's index relative to air and the interface is stationary. Does this imply that a diver cannot see surrounding objects? Which is the complete correct inference?

options.text: Yes; speed stays unchanged, so the shorter wavelength makes frequency $n$ times its air value and necessarily turns the original visible light invisible.
No; both speed and frequency decrease to $1/n$ of their air values, leaving wavelength equal to its air value and preserving visibility.
No; both frequency and speed equal their air values while wavelength falls to $1/n$, so only the spacing of wave crests changes.
No; frequency stays fixed while speed and wavelength both fall to $1/n$, retaining visible frequencies; objects remain visible when enough visible light from them reaches the eyes.

intent.task: Use the refractive index of water relative to air to relate wavelength, speed, and frequency, and decide whether the shorter wavelength makes natural light invisible.
intent.source_solution: No. For each frequency component, the stationary air-water interface preserves frequency, and the relative refractive index gives $v_{\mathrm{water}}=v_{\mathrm{air}}/n$. From $v=f\lambda$, $\lambda_{\mathrm{water}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{air}}/n$ while $f_{\mathrm{water}}=f_{\mathrm{air}}$. The shorter in-medium wavelength does not shift a visible frequency outside the visible range. A diver can still see objects when enough visible light reaches the eyes from them. This does not guarantee clear vision at every depth or turbidity, or perfectly unchanged object colours: propagation losses can change the proportions of frequencies reaching the eyes.
intent.unit_reason: Underwater visibility must be explained jointly by frequency, speed, and the given wavelength. Select a complete conclusion and reason, not a bare yes/no answer or separate quantity blanks.
limitations: Recognizing the full argument does not demonstrate unaided use of $v=f\lambda$ or composing the explanation of underwater visibility.

rationales.derivation: Wrongly keep $v_{\mathrm{water}}=v_{\mathrm{air}}$ and insert $\lambda_{\mathrm{air}}/n$ into $f=v/\lambda$, giving $f_{\mathrm{water}}=nf_{\mathrm{air}}$; then assert without justification that every component leaves the visible range. The boundary actually preserves frequency.
rationales.misconception: Combine air speed with water wavelength to calculate frequency, then treat every shortening as invisibility.

rationales.derivation: Treat slower propagation as vibrations slowing by the same factor: set $v'=v/n$ and $f'=f/n$, then obtain $\lambda'=v'/f'=\lambda$. This contradicts both frequency preservation and the given wavelength.
rationales.misconception: Conflate propagation speed and vibration frequency, dividing both by $n$ and incorrectly cancelling the wavelength change.

rationales.derivation: Preserve frequency correctly but also preserve speed incorrectly, treating the given shorter wavelength as an independent third change. Since $v=f\lambda$, fixed frequency and shorter wavelength require a proportional reduction in speed.
rationales.misconception: Accept the shorter wavelength but treat refraction as changing only direction, not speed, violating $v=f\lambda$.

rationales.derivation: The stationary boundary gives $f'=f$ and the relative index gives $v'=v/n$, hence $\lambda'=v'/f'=\lambda/n$. Visible frequencies have not become invisible ones; visibility is conditional on sufficient light reaching the eyes.

view.stem: Which arrangements correctly use interference for precise measurement, surface inspection, or improved optical imaging? Select every correct application with its stated principle.

options.text: Use an interferometer to relate a known optical-path change to fringe displacement and precisely measure light wavelength.
Choose a lens film with suitable thickness and refractive index so reflected waves weaken each other, reducing reflection and stray light to improve transmitted imaging.
Pass one interferometer beam through the gas being tested and use its optical-path change and fringe displacement to measure refractive index.
Cancel reflection in a non-absorbing lens film while creating extra light energy, making transmitted energy exceed incident energy to brighten the image.
Place a test surface near a reference plane and use changes in fringes from the two reflections to detect local path differences and inspect surface quality.
Add a green-light antireflection coating and use its pale violet reflection as evidence that it acts as a filter transmitting only violet light.

intent.task: Collectively identify the source-listed main applications, rather than recognizing antireflection alone.
intent.source_solution: Main applications include interferometers using fringe and optical-path changes for precise measurement of light wavelength, measurement of gas refractive index, and specialized tests; the source specifically lists surface-quality inspection through fringe changes. Another category is antireflection treatment of camera lenses, projector lenses, periscopes, and similar instruments: film thickness sets the reflected waves' relative phase and refractive index helps match amplitudes, reducing reflection and stray light to improve transmitted imaging. In the transparent, non-absorbing ideal model, reduced reflected energy becomes transmitted energy rather than amplified or newly created light; real losses prevent a guarantee of complete transmission. A green-light antireflection coating is not a filter transmitting only violet light.
intent.unit_reason: Listing main applications is intrinsically a collection task. One multiple-response unit collectively covers wavelength measurement, gas-index measurement, surface-quality inspection, and antireflection, without separate repetitive yes/no items or antireflection-only coverage.
limitations: Selecting supplied applications does not demonstrate unaided recall and listing of all main applications; content coverage of four applications is not evidence of free-list production.

rationales.derivation: An optical-path difference changes relative phase on the wavelength scale, and fringe displacement records that change. Relating a known path change to fringes provides wavelength information, a source-listed measurement application.

Thickness sets relative phase and refractive index affects reflected amplitudes; suitable choices weaken reflection at the selected wavelength. Reduced reflection can improve useful transmission and reduce stray reflections, without requiring complete cancellation at every colour or zero real losses.

The gas refractive index changes optical path along a given geometrical path, shifting the relative phase and fringes. Controlling the other quantities lets those changes supply gas-index information, as listed in the source.

Interpret the brighter image after reduced reflection as newly created energy, then infer transmission exceeding incidence. In the non-absorbing model, reduced reflection becomes transmission; total energy does not increase.
rationales.misconception: Mistake antireflection's redistribution of flux for optical amplification or energy creation.

rationales.derivation: In the source-listed thin-air-layer test, surface variations change local layer thickness and reflected path difference, changing or bending fringes. The option retains that phase-and-fringe inspection mechanism without a numerical precision conversion or an unselected figure.

Treat the pale violet colour of remaining reflection as the transmitted colour, then turn a change in reflected proportions into violet-only transmission. A green-light coating mainly reduces green reflection; its residual reflection does not imply transmission of violet alone.
rationales.misconception: Confuse reflection and transmission, using reflected colour proportions as the transmitted filter range.
